newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crudes firmer, but sour discount deepens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crudes firmer, but sour discount deepens.

text.p: U.S. cash crude prices firmed Tuesday afternoon as futures headed higher in anticipation of a favorable inventories report, but sour crude differentials eased off firmer levels seen earlier, traders said.

Outright crude futures prices for benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI/Cushing) traded a narrow range during the regular session between $19.45 and $19.78, settling near the top at $19.73, up 21 cents on the day.
Traders said there was an expectation that gasoline stocks would decline after the July 4 holiday weekend in the U.S. and would be reflected in Tuesday evening's American Petroleum Institute report.
In the cash market, the WTI/Cushing exchange for physical (efp) premium was unchanged at around three cents and the August/September roll was steady at around 9/10 cents contango.
Among the main domestic grades, the Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James premium gained further to trade between 20 and 24 cents as North Sea Brent remained too expensive for the Gulf market.
West Texas Sour/Midland traded several times, as high as a $1.18 discount to WTI/Cushing, but moved out to $1.17/1.27 below from $1.15/$1.17 at noon.

"Iraq being out helps but mainly it's one big short out there holding it up," said a Houston broker, explaining the improvement in sour differentials over the last month or so. The big short is an independent midwestern refiner, he said.

On Tuesday, the United Nations coordinator in Baghdad was to meet with Iraqi government officials and expected to receive an aid procurement and distribution plan. But there was no news by late afternoon in New York.

Iraq had exported around 660,000 barrels per day of its crude from December 10 to June 7 under the deal and was given permission to export for another 180 days from June 8. The Iraqi oil minister said week before last that he expected to resume exports shortly at around 730,000 to 750,000 bpd.
"There will be plenty of supply when Iraq comes back but not for at least 30 days (into the U.S. Gulf)," said a trader for a firm specializing in crude arbitrage.
The stream of sour Mars crude from the Gulf of Mexico, which reached its plateau 100,000 bpd a month or so ago, traded earlier this month at a $2.60 discount to WTI.
The weaker sour prices means the bids, which have been hard to find, for Eugene Island have moved out to $1.40 or more below WTI, traders said.
